lesson_title: One Hundred Rand of Sunshine: How the Atmosphere Gets Warm
hook_text: The sun sends earth R100 a day. Follow the money and you understand climate.
clip_script: Say the sun sends the earth one hundred rand every day. Follow the money. Thirty rand never even gets spent — it bounces straight off cloud tops, off dust, off bright ground like snow and pale desert sand. Geographers call that bounce ALBEDO. Wear a white shirt on a Kimberley afternoon and you have raised your own albedo. Twenty rand gets taken on the way in — a commission charged by ozone, water vapour and cloud. That leaves fifty rand landing on the ground. The ground is the one that actually gets paid — so the ground is the one that gets warm. Now the twist that explains everything. The ground does not keep the money. It spends it back upward, but in a different currency: sunlight arrives short-wave, and the earth, being much cooler than the sun, pays it back long-wave. And the atmosphere, which barely noticed the short-wave coming in, grabs the long-wave greedily on the way out. That is the greenhouse effect, and it is why the air near the ground is the warmest air there is.
visual_style: Rand notes falling as sunbeams, splitting into three streams that bounce, get skimmed and land; the ground glowing and paying back in a differently coloured currency that the sky catches.
mood: Streetwise clarity — money logic applied to the sky.
pacing: Crisp three-beat split of the money, slow deliberate turn on the twist.
